claim: The combined-immunotherapy of adoptive cell therapy (ACT) and cyclophosphamide (CTX) is one of the most efficient treatments for melanoma patients.
source: The combined-immunotherapy of adoptive cell therapy (ACT) and cyclophosphamide (CTX) is one of the most efficient treatments for melanoma patients.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citation to established literature on cancer immunotherapy.

claim: Regulatory T cells formed an 'immunosuppressive ring' around a solid tumor.
source: Intravital imaging data indicated that regulatory T cells formed an 'immunosuppressive ring' around a solid tumor.
evidence: This claim is supported by intravital imaging data presented in the manuscript, specifically shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1D.

claim: The CTX-ACT combined-treatment elicited synergistic immunoreactions in tumor areas, which included relieving the immune suppression, triggering the transient activation of endogenous tumor-infiltrating immunocytes, increasing the accumulation of adoptive cytotoxic T lymphocytes, and accelerating the infiltration of dendritic cells.
source: The CTX-ACT combined-treatment elicited synergistic immunoreactions in tumor areas, which included relieving the immune suppression, triggering the transient activation of endogenous tumor-infiltrating immunocytes, increasing the accumulation of adoptive cytotoxic T lymphocytes, and accelerating the infiltration of dendritic cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple intravital imaging experiments and quantitative analyses presented throughout the manuscript, including Figures 2-7.

claim: ACT has been reported to be one of the most efficient treatments for patients with melanoma because it effectively elicits anti-tumor immune responses and leads to objective tumor regression in more than 50% of patients (Pittet et al., 2007; Rosenberg et al., 2008).
source: ACT has been reported to be one of the most efficient treatments for patients with melanoma because it effectively elicits anti-tumor immune responses and leads to objective tumor regression in more than 50% of patients (Pittet et al., 2007; Rosenberg et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: The ACT treatment failed to control the tumor growth.
source: However, the ACT treatment failed to control the tumor growth (Figure 1A), which is consistent with the results reported for certain clinical cases (Zippelius et al., 2004; Mukai et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and is consistent with cited clinical cases.

claim: Adoptive CTLs primarily accumulated in the TDLNs but rarely accumulated in the tumors during either the early or the late stage.
source: The data indicated that the CTLs primarily accumulated in the TDLNs but rarely accumulated in the tumors during either the early or the late stage (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from frozen tissue sections shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Only a few CFSE-labeled adoptive CTLs infiltrated into the tumor area, regardless of an early or late stage post-adoptive CTL transfer.
source: The intravital imaging data revealed that only a few CFSE-labeled adoptive CTLs infiltrated into the tumor area, regardless of an early or late stage post-adoptive CTL transfer (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Tregs (Foxp3-mRFP cells) were clearly observed infiltrating the tumor microenvironment on Day 1, before they gradually accumulated at the edge of the tumor to form a ring on Day 5.
source: Compared with the rare infiltration of adoptive CTLs, Tregs (Foxp3-mRFP cells) were clearly observed infiltrating the tumor microenvironment on Day 1, before they gradually accumulated at the edge of the tumor to form a ring on Day 5 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal intravital imaging data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: An 'immunosuppressive ring' formed by Tregs surrounded the solid tumor to prevent the recruitment of adoptive CTLs.
source: This observation suggested that an 'immunosuppressive ring' formed by Tregs surrounded the solid tumor to prevent the recruitment of adoptive CTLs, as illustrated in the schematic diagram in Figure 1D.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the imaging data, supported by the observed spatial distribution of Tregs and CTLs.

claim: The dose of 150 mg kg−1 CTX controlled the CFP-B16 tumor growth successfully when CTX was used alone as well as when it was used in combination with ACT.
source: The results of these experiments showed that, compared with other CTX doses (50 mg kg−1 and 100 mg kg−1) usually used in tumor immunotherapy, only the dose of 150 mg kg−1 CTX controlled the CFP-B16 tumor growth successfully when CTX was used alone as well as when it was used in combination with ACT (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth inhibition experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The effective anti-tumor effect of CTX at the dose of 150 mg kg−1 is not due to its direct cytotoxicity.
source: Furthermore, a tumor growth inhibition experiment performed on the BALB/c nude mice, confirmed that the effective anti-tumor effect of CTX at the dose of 150 mg kg−1 is not due to its direct cytotoxicity, because no difference in the inhibition of tumor growth was observed between the PBS control group and the mice treated with different doses of CTX (50, 100 or 150 mg kg−1, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments in immune-deficient nude mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The efficacy of the 150 mg kg−1 CTX treatment for CFP-B16 tumor in C57BL/6 mice depends on the enhanced anti-tumor immune response, and not on the direct cytotoxicity of the treatment.
source: These results suggest that the efficacy of the 150 mg kg−1 CTX treatment for CFP-B16 tumor in C57BL/6 mice depends on the enhanced anti-tumor immune response, and not on the direct cytotoxicity of the treatment.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the comparison of CTX effects in immune-competent versus immune-deficient mice.

claim: The CTX-ACT combined treatment significantly inhibited tumor growth compared with the ACT treatment alone, but produced results that were not significantly different from those produced by the CTX treatment alone.
source: The CTX-ACT combined treatment significantly inhibited tumor growth compared with the ACT treatment alone, but produced results that were not significantly different from those produced by the CTX treatment alone (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth curve data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The CTX treatment successfully eliminated most of the Tregs in the tumor area and removed the 'immunosuppressive ring' formed by Tregs.
source: The CTX treatment successfully eliminated most of the Tregs in the tumor area and removed the 'immunosuppressive ring' formed by Tregs (Figure 2B, bottom left corner).
evidence: This claim is supported by intravital imaging and immunohistochemical staining shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The number of CFSE-labeled CTLs in the tumor area was clearly increased in CTX-ACT-treated mice, compared with that in mice received the ACT treatment alone.
source: In addition, the number of CFSE-labeled CTLs in the tumor area was clearly increased in CTX-ACT-treated mice, compared with that in mice received the ACT treatment alone (Figure 2B, left panel, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging and quantitative data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The accumulation of CTLs increased significantly during the late stage (Days 4–6).
source: These images showed that in the combined treatment, few adoptive CTLs infiltrated into the tumor microenvironment during the early stage (Days 1–3). Subsequently, the accumulation of CTLs increased significantly during the late stage (Days 4–6, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by longitudinal intravital imaging data shown in Figure 2C and quantified in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The infiltrating CTLs destroyed the solid tumor by applying two approaches: attacking the tumor cells at the periphery according to an 'outside-in' pattern and eliminating tumor cells at the parenchyma according to an 'inside-out' pattern.
source: This finding suggested that the infiltrating CTLs destroyed the solid tumor by applying two approaches: attacking the tumor cells at the periphery according to an 'outside-in' pattern and eliminating tumor cells at the parenchyma according to an 'inside-out' pattern.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the imaging data showing tumor destruction patterns.

claim: The anti-tumor effect of the adoptive CTLs peaked at Days 5–6.
source: The anti-tumor effect of the adoptive CTLs peaked at Days 5–6.
evidence: This claim is supported by the imaging data showing maximum tumor destruction at these time points.

claim: One day later (Figure 2C, Day 7), the number of adoptive CTLs decreased rapidly in the tumor area because of the death or dysfunction of CTLs, leading to tumor regrowth.
source: One day later (Figure 2C, Day 7), the number of adoptive CTLs decreased rapidly in the tumor area because of the death or dysfunction of CTLs, leading to tumor regrowth.
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 2C and is an inference about the mechanism of CTL decrease.

claim: During the first stage (Days 1–2), a number of adoptive CTLs migrated to the tumor periphery with a mean velocity of 3.23 ± 2.18 µm min−1 and only a few CTLs infiltrated into the tumor parenchyma.
source: The first stage corresponds to Days 1–2. During this stage, a number of adoptive CTLs migrated to the tumor periphery (Figure 3A, Day 1) with a mean velocity of 3.23 ± 2.18 µm min−1 (n = 80 cells from 4–5 mice, Figure 3F) and only a few CTLs infiltrated into the tumor parenchyma (Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of CTL motility shown in Figure 3 and Video 1.

claim: During the second stage (Days 3–4), adoptive CTLs accumulated at the periphery of the tumor with a mean velocity of 3.13 ± 2.43 µm min−1, confinement ratio of 0.57 ± 0.29, and arrest coefficient of 48 ± 36%.
source: The second stage corresponds to Days 3–4. During this stage, adoptive CTLs accumulated at the periphery of the tumor (mean velocity – 3.13 ± 2.43 µm min−1, confinement ratio – 0.57 ± 0.29, and arrest coefficient – 48 ± 36%, n = 305 cells; Figure 3A,F–H, Day 3) and their motility was similar to that at Day 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative motility analysis shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: A few of adoptive CTLs were able to infiltrate into the tumor parenchyma during Days 3-4, and remained confined with constrained trajectories and slow speed (mean velocity – 0.87 ± 0.28 µm min−1, confinement ratio – 0.32 ± 0.21, and arrest coefficient – 91 ± 8%).
source: Nevertheless, a few of adoptive CTLs were able to infiltrate into the tumor parenchyma, and remained confined with constrained trajectories (Figure 3C,D) and slow speed (mean velocity – 0.87 ± 0.28 µm min−1, confinement ratio – 0.32 ± 0.21, and arrest coefficient – 91 ± 8%; n = 118 cells; Figure 3F–H), suggesting that these CTLs formed stable interactions with neighboring tumor cells (Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative motility data and imaging shown in Figure 3 and Video 2.

claim: During the third stage (Day 5), a larger number of adoptive CTLs migrated to the tumor periphery and their mean velocity dramatically increased to 5.79 ± 3.12 µm min−1.
source: During the third stage (Day 5), a larger number of adoptive CTLs migrated to the tumor periphery and their mean velocity dramatically increased to 5.79 ± 3.12 µm min−1 (n = 428 cells), which was much faster than the mean velocities calculated during the first two stages (p<0.001; Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative motility analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The CTLs in the deep tumor parenchyma on Day 5 displayed a trend toward greater speed with a marked increase in their mean velocity to 3.22 ± 2.58 µm min−1.
source: The CTLs in the deep tumor parenchyma also displayed a trend toward greater speed with a marked increase in their mean velocity to 3.22 ± 2.58 µm min−1 (n = 193 cells; Figure 3F), less confined trajectories (confinement ratio – 0.60 ± 0.25; Figure 3B,G) and a decrease in the arrest coefficient (50 ± 39%; Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative motility data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: When most tumor cells were killed, the adoptive CTLs resumed their high-speed movement to search for new targets.
source: The changes in the migratory behavior of the CTLs in both tumor periphery and parenchyma were consistent with the observed tumor destruction (Figures 2C and 3C, Video 3), indicating that when most tumor cells were killed, the adoptive CTLs resumed their high-speed movement to search for new targets.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the correlation between CTL motility and tumor destruction.

claim: During the fourth stage (Day 6), the motility of CTLs near the tumor periphery remained high (mean velocity – 5.89 ± 3.9 µm min−1, confinement ratio – 0.69 ± 0.24, and arrest coefficient – 26 ± 34%).
source: During the fourth stage (Day 6), the motility of CTLs near the tumor periphery remained high (mean velocity – 5.89 ± 3.9 µm min−1, confinement ratio – 0.69 ± 0.24, and arrest coefficient – 26 ± 34%; n = 147 cells; Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative motility data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: The motility of CTLs in the parenchyma on Day 6 significantly decreased as evidenced by their more confined trajectories and an obvious increase in the arrest coefficient (mean velocity – 0.86 ± 1.49 µm min−1, confinement ratio – 0.46 ± 0.22, and arrest coefficient – 88 ± 29%).
source: By contrast, the motility of CTLs in the parenchyma significantly decreased as evidenced by their more confined trajectories and an obvious increase in the arrest coefficient (mean velocity – 0.86 ± 1.49 µm min−1, confinement ratio – 0.46 ± 0.22, and arrest coefficient – 88 ± 29%; Figure 3F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative motility data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: The decreased number and motility of the CTLs and tumor regrowth suggested that the adoptive CTLs were dysfunctional or died during the fourth stage.
source: The decreased number and motility of the CTLs and tumor regrowth suggested that the adoptive CTLs were dysfunctional or died during this stage (Video 4).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed decrease in CTL number and motility correlated with tumor regrowth.

claim: All of the adoptive CTLs in both the tumor periphery and the tumor parenchyma displayed random walking during different stages.
source: The mean displacement analysis revealed that all of the adoptive CTLs in both the tumor periphery and the tumor parenchyma displayed random walking during different stages (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mean displacement analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The migratory behavior of adoptive CTLs in the tumor areas at different stages is correlated to their anti-tumor efficacy.
source: These data suggested that the migratory behavior of adoptive CTLs in the tumor areas at different stages is correlated to their anti-tumor efficacy.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the correlation between CTL motility patterns and tumor destruction.

claim: A subsequent round of CTX-ACT combined treatment is required to maintain the anti-tumor immune activation.
source: The dysfunction and death of adoptive CTLs and tumor regrowth during the fourth stage suggested that a subsequent round of CTX-ACT combined treatment is required to maintain the anti-tumor immune activation.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed CTL dysfunction and tumor regrowth.

claim: The endogenous GFP cells in the tumors decreased after CTX-ACT treatment.
source: The data showed that the endogenous GFP cells in the tumors decreased after CTX-ACT treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Most of the GFP cells in the tumors of the CTX-ACT-treated mice were CD8+ CTLs with expression of the activation marker CD69 (more than 60%).
source: Importantly, most of the GFP cells in the tumors of the CTX-ACT-treated mice were CD8+ CTLs with expression of the activation marker CD69 (more than 60%, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The CTX-ACT combined treatment decreased the endogenous T cells but selectively retained the activated endogenous CD8+ CTLs in the tumors.
source: These results suggest that the CTX-ACT combined treatment decreased the endogenous T cells but selectively retained the activated endogenous CD8+ CTLs in the tumors.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the flow cytometry data showing decreased total GFP cells but enriched CD8+CD69+ cells.

claim: The number of endogenous GFP T cells in the tumor area of CTX-ACT-treated mice was much smaller than that in ACT-treated mice.
source: Intravital imaging showed that the number of endogenous GFP T cells in the tumor area of CTX-ACT-treated mice was much smaller than that in ACT-treated mice (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by intravital imaging and quantification shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Compared with the ACT group, the motility of the endogenous GFP T cells in the tumor areas of the CTX-ACT group was significantly decreased with more confined trajectories and a significantly increased arrest coefficient.
source: The analysis of the migratory behavior of the endogenous T cells showed that, compared with the ACT group, the motility of the endogenous GFP T cells in the tumor areas of the CTX-ACT group was significantly decreased (Video 5), with more confined trajectories and a significantly increased arrest coefficient (mean velocity – 3.80 ± 2.56 µm min−1 in the CTX-ACT group versus 4.6 ± 2.0 µm min−1 in the ACT group; confinement ratio – 0.47 ± 0.26 in the CTX-ACT group versus 0.60 ± 0.25 in the ACT group; and arrest coefficient – 43 ± 35% in the CTX-ACT group versus 25 ± 26% in the ACT group; Figure 4C–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative motility analysis shown in Figure 4C-F and Video 5.

claim: The activated endogenous CTLs arrested in the tumor area for a long time and built stable, long-lasting interactions with the tumor cells to kill them efficiently.
source: The activated endogenous CTLs arrested in the tumor area for a long time and built stable, long-lasting interactions with the tumor cells to kill them efficiently.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed decreased motility and increased arrest coefficient of endogenous CTLs.

claim: On Day 1, the endogenous TIIs in the CTX-ACT-treated mice migrated rapidly toward the tumor parenchyma with a mean velocity of 4.92 ± 2.80 µm min−1.
source: On Day 1, the endogenous TIIs in the CTX-ACT-treated mice migrated rapidly toward the tumor parenchyma (mean velocity – 4.92 ± 2.80 µm min−1; n = 435 cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative motility analysis of TIIs.

claim: The velocity of TIIs on Day 1 (24 hr after CTX-ACT treatment) was approximately 2.4-fold faster than that on Day 0.
source: The velocity on Day 1 (24 hr after CTX-ACT treatment, Figure 5B–D, Video 6) was approximately 2.4-fold faster than that on Day 0 (2.07 ± 2.18 µm min−1, n = 477 cells; Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison of TII velocities shown in Figure 5D.

claim: A transient increase in the motility of the endogenous TIIs was induced within 24 hr after the CTX-ACT treatment.
source: Thus, a transient increase in the motility of the endogenous TIIs was induced within 24 hr after the CTX-ACT treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the time-course analysis of TII motility showing peak velocity at Day 1.

claim: Day 1 is a key point in time for the activation of endogenous anti-tumor immune reactions in response to the CTX-ACT combined treatment.
source: These findings indicate that Day 1 is a key point in time for the activation of endogenous anti-tumor immune reactions in response to the CTX-ACT combined treatment.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed peak in TII motility at Day 1.

claim: The tumor destruction was caused by both adoptive CTLs and endogenous TIIs.
source: We speculated that the tumor destruction was caused by both adoptive CTLs and endogenous TIIs.
evidence: This claim is explicitly stated as speculation based on the observed activation of both cell types.

claim: The chemotaxis of the endogenous TIIs toward the tumor parenchyma was elicited only by the CTX-ACT treatment.
source: Analysis of the imaging data and migratory path indicated that the chemotaxis of the endogenous TIIs toward the tumor parenchyma was elicited only by the CTX-ACT treatment (Figure 6A, B, Video 7), which caused the TII movement to display long and linear trajectories (confinement ratio – 0.66 ± 0.25, Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of TII trajectories across different treatment groups shown in Figure 6.

claim: The endogenous TIIs in the CTX-ACT treatment group displayed the greatest motility with the fastest mean velocity (4.92 ± 2.80 µm min−1) and the lowest arrest coefficient (21 ± 21%).
source: The endogenous TIIs in the CTX-ACT treatment group displayed the greatest motility with the fastest mean velocity (4.92 ± 2.80 µm min−1; Figure 6C) and the lowest arrest coefficient (21 ± 21%, Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative motility analysis shown in Figure 6C and 6E.

claim: The CTX-ACT treatment had a synergistic effect on the activation of endogenous TIIs, which in return accelerated the anti-tumor effects of the adoptive CTLs.
source: Among all of these groups, only the CTX-ACT treatment group exhibited the movement of TIIs toward the tumor parenchyma with high motility and expanded trajectories. These findings indicate that the CTX-ACT treatment had a synergistic effect on the activation of endogenous TIIs, which in return accelerated the anti-tumor effects of the adoptive CTLs.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the unique TII activation pattern observed only in the CTX-ACT group.

claim: Most of the tumor-surrounding EGFP cells were Ly6G+ cells.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of the frozen tumor sections showed that most of the tumor-surrounding EGFP cells were Ly6G+ cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: More than 50% of the immunocytes surrounding the tumors were neutrophils.
source: Hematoxylin and eosin (HE) staining further confirmed that more than 50% of the immunocytes surrounding the tumors were neutrophils (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by HE staining and quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The CTX-ACT treatment triggered the activity of endogenous neutrophils in the anti-tumor immune response rapidly, just 24 hr after the CTX-ACT treatment (Day 1).
source: These results indicated that the CTX-ACT treatment triggered the activity of endogenous neutrophils in the anti-tumor immune response rapidly, just 24 hr after the CTX-ACT treatment (Day 1).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the identification of neutrophils as the major TII population and their rapid activation at Day 1.

claim: Many DCs infiltrated into the tumor areas of the CTX-ACT-treated mice on Day 3.
source: The imaging data showed that many DCs infiltrated into the tumor areas of the CTX-ACT-treated mice on Day 3 (three days after CTX-ACT treatment, Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by intravital imaging data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The density of the DCs in the CTX-ACT group increased by 3.6-fold compared with that in the PBS group, by 2.0-fold compared with that in the CTL group and by 1.6-fold compared with that in the CTX group.
source: The density of the DCs in the CTX-ACT group increased by 3.6-fold compared with that in the PBS group, by 2.0-fold compared with that in the CTL group and by 1.6-fold compared with that in the CTX group (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of DC density shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Certain YFP-labeled DCs displayed an mature phenotype characterized by the expression of MHC-II and CD86.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of the frozen tumor sections from CTX-ACT-treated mice revealed that certain YFP-labeled DCs displayed an mature phenotype characterized by the expression of MHC-II and CD86, indicating that some mature DCs were present in the tumor areas (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The CTX-ACT treatment promotes the infiltration of DCs (some of them were mature) to the tumor areas to further enhance the anti-tumor effects.
source: This finding suggests that the CTX-ACT treatment promotes the infiltration of DCs (some of them were mature) to the tumor areas to further enhance the anti-tumor effects.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the observed increase in DC infiltration and presence of mature DCs.

claim: The motility of the adoptive CTLs remained at a high level on Day 5 both at the tumor periphery and in the parenchyma.
source: According to the intravital imaging data, the motility of the adoptive CTLs remained at a high level on Day 5 both at the tumor periphery and in the parenchyma (Figure 3A–D, Video 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by motility analysis shown in Figure 3A-D and Video 3.

claim: The anti-tumor response peaked on Day 5.
source: Concomitant with this phenomenon, the anti-tumor response also peaked on Day 5 (Figure 2C, Figure 3A,C), and then the tumor continued to grow (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by imaging data showing maximum tumor destruction at Day 5.

claim: An effective interval time of five days between treatment rounds was determined for the CTX-ACT combined therapy.
source: According to these results, an effective interval time of five days between treatment rounds was determined for the CTX-ACT combined therapy.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the timing of CTL activation and anti-tumor response peaks.

claim: The metronomic treatments controlled the growth of the tumor during its entire course, with a significantly more effective tumor growth control compared with the other control groups that received only a single round of the CTX-ACT treatment (p<0.001) and the metronomic CTX treatment (p<0.05).
source: When administered three times successfully, the metronomic treatments controlled the growth of the tumor during its entire course, with a significantly more effective tumor growth control compared with the other control groups that received only a single round of the CTX-ACT treatment (p<0.001, Figure 8B) and the metronomic CTX treatment (p<0.05, Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth curve data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The immunosuppressive ring of Tregs blocked the ability of adoptive CTLs to recognize the cognate antigen of tumor cells and decreased the migration of these CTLs into the tumor area.
source: Thus, we propose that the immunosuppressive ring of Tregs blocked the ability of adoptive CTLs to recognize the cognate antigen of tumor cells and decreased the migration of these CTLs into the tumor area.
evidence: This claim is a proposed mechanism based on the observed spatial distribution of Tregs and CTLs.

claim: The depletion of the Tregs induced by CTX treatment contributed to the accumulation of adoptive CTLs in the tumor area in three ways: (1) it cleared the immunosuppressive barrier to facilitate the migration of adoptive CTLs into the tumor area; (2) it induced the elevated expression of some chemokines and cytokines in the tumor microenvironment to promote the accumulation of adoptive CTLs (Bracci et al., 2007; Schiavoni et al., 2011); and (3) it provided space to allow the infiltration and homeostatic proliferation of adoptive CTLs (Bracci et al., 2007; Sistigu et al., 2011).
source: Additionally, the depletion of the Tregs induced by CTX treatment contributed to the accumulation of adoptive CTLs in the tumor area in three ways: (1) it cleared the immunosuppressive barrier to facilitate the migration of adoptive CTLs into the tumor area; (2) it induced the elevated expression of some chemokines and cytokines in the tumor microenvironment to promote the accumulation of adoptive CTLs (Bracci et al., 2007; Schiavoni et al., 2011); and (3) it provided space to allow the infiltration and homeostatic proliferation of adoptive CTLs (Bracci et al., 2007; Sistigu et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim combines data from the current study with cited mechanisms from previous literature.

claim: The infiltrated DCs may take up tumor antigens and present them to T cells (Restifo et al., 2012) to further elicit the anti-tumor immune response.
source: This phenomenon suggests that the infiltrated DCs may take up tumor antigens and present them to T cells (Restifo et al., 2012) to further elicit the anti-tumor immune response.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about DC function based on their observed infiltration timing and cited literature.

claim: The CTX-ACT combined treatment displayed synergistic anti-tumor effects by blocking the formation of an immunosuppressive ring around solid tumors by Tregs, eliciting the transient migratory activity of TIIs toward the tumor parenchyma, and accelerating the infiltration of adoptive CTLs and endogenous DCs into the tumor.
source: In summary, the CTX-ACT combined treatment displayed synergistic anti-tumor effects by blocking the formation of an immunosuppressive ring around solid tumors by Tregs, eliciting the transient migratory activity of TIIs toward the tumor parenchyma, and accelerating the infiltration of adoptive CTLs and endogenous DCs into the tumor.
evidence: This claim summarizes the main findings supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: The CTX-ACT treatment not only promoted the anti-tumor effects of adoptive CTLs but also elicited endogenous anti-tumor immune responses.
source: The CTX-ACT treatment not only promoted the anti-tumor effects of adoptive CTLs but also elicited endogenous anti-tumor immune responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing activation of both adoptive CTLs and endogenous immune cells.

claim: Three rounds of metronomic CTX-ACT treatments successfully controlled the tumor growth for several weeks.
source: Guided by the results obtained by intravital imaging, three rounds of metronomic CTX-ACT treatments successfully controlled the tumor growth for several weeks.
evidence: This claim is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: mCerulean (CFP-B16 tumor cells) is minimally immunogenic in C57BL/6 mice (Skelton et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2016).
source: Here, the activity and cytotoxicity of CTLs against target tumor cells were demonstrated in vitro by flow cytometry of B16 tumor cells that stably express mutants of the cyan fluorescent protein mCerulean (CFP-B16 tumor cells, Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is minimally immunogenic in C57BL/6 mice (Skelton et al., 2001; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cancer immunotherapy has been an area of significant process in recent decades, and is considered a breakthrough in cancer therapy (Couzin-Frankel, 2013).
source: Cancer immunotherapy has been an area of significant process in recent decades, and is considered a breakthrough in cancer therapy (Couzin-Frankel, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Current promising techniques in cancer immunotherapy are the use of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), tumor vaccines, and adoptive cell therapy (ACT) (Elert, 2013; Couzin-Frankel and McNutt, 2013).
source: Current promising techniques in cancer immunotherapy are the use of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), tumor vaccines, and adoptive cell therapy (ACT) (Elert, 2013; Couzin-Frankel and McNutt, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) play a key immunosuppressive role in the endogenous immunosuppressive networks (Curiel et al., 2004; Vignali et al., 2008).
source: Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Tregs) play a key immunosuppressive role in the endogenous immunosuppressive networks (Curiel et al., 2004; Vignali et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cyclophosphamide (CTX) is a commonly used alkylating agent in chemotherapy, which has been applied in recent years to selectively suppress, abrogate and deplete Tregs before ACT treatment (Rosenberg et al., 2008; Nishikawa and Sakaguchi, 2014; Oleinika et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2010).
source: Cyclophosphamide (CTX) is a commonly used alkylating agent in chemotherapy, which has been applied in recent years to selectively suppress, abrogate and deplete Tregs before ACT treatment (Rosenberg et al., 2008; Nishikawa and Sakaguchi, 2014; Oleinika et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lymphodepletion before ACT by CTX treatment further promoted tumor-specific CTL infiltration into the target tumors (Bracci et al., 2007; Rosenberg et al., 2008; Boissonnas et al., 2013).
source: Lymphodepletion before ACT by CTX treatment further promoted tumor-specific CTL infiltration into the target tumors (Bracci et al., 2007; Rosenberg et al., 2008; Boissonnas et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The migratory behavior of effector T cells in solid tumors has been analyzed by two-photon microscopy, proving that migration presents the critical step for the sufficient infiltration of T cells into the solid tumor and promotes tumor elimination (Mrass et al., 2006; Boissonnas et al., 2007).
source: The migratory behavior of effector T cells in solid tumors has been analyzed by two-photon microscopy, proving that migration presents the critical step for the sufficient infiltration of T cells into the solid tumor and promotes tumor elimination (Mrass et al., 2006; Boissonnas et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous imaging studies.

claim: Other immunomodulatory mechanisms of CTX treatment include the systemic activation of DCs (Radojcic et al., 2010; Veltman et al., 2010; Nakahara et al., 2010), increase of the infiltration of DCs into the tumor area (Schiavoni et al., 2011), and promotion of the penetration of CTLs into the tumor parenchyma (Boissonnas et al., 2013; Bracci et al., 2007).
source: In addition to the selective depletion and suppression of Tregs, other immunomodulatory mechanisms of CTX treatment include the systemic activation of DCs (Radojcic et al., 2010; Veltman et al., 2010; Nakahara et al., 2010), increase of the infiltration of DCs into the tumor area (Schiavoni et al., 2011), and promotion of the penetration of CTLs into the tumor parenchyma (Boissonnas et al., 2013; Bracci et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A large number of DCs infiltrating into the tumor parenchyma has been shown to have a positive association with longer survival of cancer patients (Chaput et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2005; Pagès et al., 2010).
source: A large number of DCs infiltrating into the tumor parenchyma has been shown to have a positive association with longer survival of cancer patients (Chaput et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2005; Pagès et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs) play dichotomous roles because they exhibit both pro-tumor and anti-tumor effects during tumor progression (Mantovani et al., 2011; Piccard et al., 2012; Brandau et al., 2013).
source: In recent years, the interest in tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs) has increased, and accumulating data have demonstrated that TANs play dichotomous roles because they exhibit both pro-tumor and anti-tumor effects during tumor progression (Mantovani et al., 2011; Piccard et al., 2012; Brandau et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on TANs.

claim: During the early stage of tumor progression, accumulating TANs with high motility (also described as TENs (Granot et al., 2011)), play an important role in the anti-tumor response by exerting a direct cytotoxic effect on tumor cells (Hicks et al., 2006), enhancing antibody-induced anti-tumor effects (Albanesi et al., 2013), and having a stimulatory effect on T cell proliferation (Eruslanov et al., 2014).
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that during the early stage of tumor progression, accumulating TANs with high motility ((Yao et al., 2015), also described as TENs (Granot et al., 2011)), play an important role in the anti-tumor response by exerting a direct cytotoxic effect on tumor cells (Hicks et al., 2006), enhancing antibody-induced anti-tumor effects (Albanesi et al., 2013), and having a stimulatory effect on T cell proliferation (Eruslanov et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on neutrophil functions.

claim: CTLs must recognize the cognate antigen of tumor cells before they are able to infiltrate into the tumor parenchyma sufficiently (Boissonnas et al., 2007; Mrass et al., 2006).
